claims.note: Title and description present the page as a capability-envelope guide with an auditable session record. The count in them ('four separate controls, and only three are enforced by the system rather than by the agent's own behaviour') matches the article's own table and topic sentence: row 1 is the agent's policy loop, rows 2-4 (interface scope, database transaction mode, runtime expression guard) are enforced outside it. No vendor result, ranking, price or measured performance claim is made here.

Analytical taxonomy asserted by this article: the four enforcement layers and the claim that only the credential scope, transaction mode and runtime guard are enforced outside the agent. No figure is asserted.
Section heading introducing three documented leak classes; each specific claim is sourced in the paragraph that carries it, and the heading itself asserts no fact.

Restates the CDP Runtime.evaluate definition of throwOnSideEffect ("if side effect cannot be ruled out") and its experimental marker, both re-read from the protocol JSON in this run; the purity caveat is an interpretation of that wording, and the article claims no test.

Restates sys.monitoring availability in 3.12, its event callbacks and integer tool identifiers from the Python docs, and explicitly declines to present it as a read-only guarantee, matching the documented scope.

Field names are quoted verbatim from this run's observed.json audit.fields_declared and set beside the article's recommended table: the fixture has no run ID apart from the session and no redaction-event, retention/immutability or side-effect-assertion field, which the paragraph now states outright. The 9-of-13 non-null count and the four null-somewhere fields are computed from the same file; the design-bug reading is labelled as interpretation.

run.methodology: Scripted client (no language model) drove nine tool calls through the envelope.json policy gate after a seeded SQLite database with PRAGMA query_only; fixture_check.py wrote one record per call to observed.json. Declared field names were read from audit.fields_declared; coverage was computed as "non-null on every record" over those 13 fields.

run.methodology: Single run of fixture_check.py on 2026-11-16 with Python 3.12.3 / SQLite 3.45.1; the CREATE TEMP TABLE probe and the follow-up insert are recorded verbatim in database_layer, including error text.

claims.note: Product surfaces (manual probes in VS Code vs an MCP-connected agent) are attributed to the vendor's How It Works page, which was fetched live and names both workflows; the default-probe description and the Node/Python/Java conditional-probe rules remain attributed to the founder's Launch HN answer. Vendor self-description, dated and not independently tested.

Follows the founder's own worked example from the Launch HN thread: `total > 50` allowed, `order.total > 50` refused because a property may invoke a getter, method invocations refused for Python/Java. The paragraph still states that the permitted operator subset is not enumerated in the thread.

Ten-step operational checklist assembled by this article from the layer analysis: credential scoping, default READ ONLY transaction mode, connection-level caps, deny-by-default allowlist, expression guard, EXPLAIN vs ANALYZE, redaction, the audit fields, session caps and a revocation switch. Prescriptive, no measurement claimed.

numbers.note: Every numeric assertion re-derived: 6 of 7 database probes refused (five readonly-database errors plus one 'no such table: scratch'), 9 tool calls with 4 allowed / 5 denied / 4 rules, 13 declared audit fields with 9 populated and 4 named nulls, 6 seeded rows and an unchanged fingerprint. Reproduced by an independent rerun of fixture_check.py on 2026-11-16.
